label: The Projective Plane P^2
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 25 through 64 and builds the two-dimensional projective plane that underlies all of multiple view geometry. We represent points and lines as homogeneous three-vectors so that parallel lines meet, joins and intersections become cross products, and one algebra serves every incidence question on the plane.

label: Points and Lines in Homogeneous Coordinates
notes: A homogeneous three-vector represents a point only up to nonzero scale, so the equivalence class is what matters. The same vectors name lines, and incidence reduces to a single dot product vanishing. Emphasize that the trailing coordinate distinguishes finite points from ideal directions at infinity.

label: Duality: Join and Meet as Cross Products
notes: Stress the symmetry between points and lines. The line through two points and the intersection of two lines are both cross products, so any true statement stays true after swapping the words point and line. This duality is the single most labor-saving idea in the projective toolbox.

label: Ideal Points and the Line at Infinity
notes: Walk through why parallel lines meet at an ideal point whose last coordinate is zero. All ideal points lie on one special line at infinity. A homography can send that line to a finite vanishing line, which is exactly how perspective images fold infinity into the picture.

label: Conics and Dual Conics
notes: Introduce the point conic as a symmetric matrix and the dual conic of tangent lines as its inverse. Show that five points fix a conic. The pole-polar relation packages tangency, polar lines of exterior points, and the contact-point geometry into one matrix-vector product.

label: Projective Transformations (Homographies)
notes: Define a homography as an invertible three-by-three matrix acting on homogeneous points up to scale, giving eight degrees of freedom. Make the action on lines explicit: lines transform by the inverse transpose, and conics by a congruence. These three rules cover every object on the plane.

label: Homographies Preserve Incidence and Cross-Ratio
notes: A homography may bend the visual spacing of a grid but never turns a line into a curve. On a single line it induces a one-dimensional projectivity, so the cross-ratio of four collinear points survives even though distances and ratios of distances along the line change.

label: The Transformation Hierarchy
notes: Lay out the ladder from projective down through affine and similarity to Euclidean. Each rung adds constraints to the matrix and gains invariants: length, angle, parallelism, area ratio, cross-ratio. Reading the hierarchy by what each level preserves makes the whole chapter memorable.

label: Invariants at Each Level
notes: Connect each subgroup to a fixed geometric object. Projectivities fix nothing special; affinities fix the line at infinity as a set; similarities and Euclidean maps additionally fix the circular points. The invariants form a nested ladder, with each named quantity surviving exactly the maps below it.

label: Affine Rectification from the Vanishing Line
notes: A perspective image of a plane differs from the plane by a homography. Two vanishing points join to give the imaged line at infinity. Mapping that line back to its canonical position removes the projective part, so parallelism and ratios of areas become measurable in the rectified chart.

label: Metric Rectification and the Circular Points
notes: After affine rectification the line at infinity is fixed but the circular points are not. The residual distortion is a symmetric positive definite two-by-two matrix, and each known right angle gives one linear constraint. Its inverse square root removes anisotropy, leaving only a similarity ambiguity.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: Tie the threads together: homogeneous coordinates unify incidence, points and lines transform by different rules, the cross-ratio is the basic projective invariant, the line at infinity carries affine structure, and the circular points carry metric structure. Conic polarity and fixed eigenstructure are the same algebra on different objects.
